Q: SELECT INTO breaks DDL/DML trigger but CREATE TABLE followed by INSERT works? A:

Based on schema changed after the target table was created. rerun the select into query

SELECT *
INTO target_tab
FROM source_tab;

It is executed in two operations create table + insert into and if anything modifies the table in between errors 539 occurs:

Schema changed after the target table was created. Rerun the Select Into query.

Example of SELECT * INTO ... FROM ... there are 2 operations:


CREATE TABLE src(i INT);
INSERT INTO src(i) VALUES(1);

SELECT i/0 AS col
INTO tab
FROM src;
--Msg 8134 Level 16 State 1 Line 1
--Divide by zero error encountered.
--Msg 3621 Level 0 State 0 Line 1
--The statement has been terminated.

SELECT * FROM tab;
-- col

-- table was created even if the previous statement failed

db<>fiddle demo

SELECT INTO - Remarks

The SELECT...INTO statement operates in two parts: the new table is created, and then rows are inserted. This two-step process means that if the inserts fail, the operation rolls back all the inserts, but the new (empty) table remains. If you need the entire operation to succeed or fail as a whole, use an explicit transaction.

In question's case:

SELECT * 
INTO [input].[secondtest] 
FROM [input].[firsttest];

Execution order:

1. CREATE [input].[secondtest]  ...
2. Database trigger CreateDMLTriggerOnTable fires
   2a. CREATE TABLE [output].[secondtest] 
   2b. CREATE TRIGGER InsertState_secondtest -- ERROR 539 (Modifying table)
3. INSERT INTO  [input].[secondtest] ...

We can confirm this by commenting out CREATE TRIGGER InsertState_secondtest:

CREATE TRIGGER CreateDMLTriggerOnTable 
ON DATABASE
AFTER CREATE_TABLE
AS
BEGIN
  DECLARE @schemaname AS SYSNAME = 'input';
  --Only act on tables in our target scheme [input]
  IF EVENTDATA().value('(/EVENT_INSTANCE/SchemaName)[1]','SYSNAME') <> @schemaname 
    RETURN;

  DECLARE @tablename AS SYSNAME = EVENTDATA().value('(/EVENT_INSTANCE/ObjectName)[1]','SYSNAME');
  DECLARE @tb_input AS VARCHAR(261) = '[input].' + QUOTENAME(@tablename);
  DECLARE @tb_output AS VARCHAR(261) = '[output].' + QUOTENAME(@tablename);

  --Create a matching [output] table for the newly created [input] table
  DECLARE @tmpsql AS NVARCHAR(MAX) = 'CREATE TABLE ' + @tb_output + '(CountOfRows INT);';
  PRINT COALESCE(@tmpsql,'NULLED!');
  EXEC(@tmpsql);
  
  --Populate [output] with data from [input] table using DML trigger
  SET @tmpsql = 'CREATE TRIGGER InsertState_' + @tablename + ' ON ' + @tb_input + ' FOR INSERT AS' + CHAR(13);
  SET @tmpsql += 'INSERT INTO ' + @tb_output + '(CountOfRows) SELECT COUNT(*) AS CountOfRows FROM inserted;';
  PRINT COALESCE(@tmpsql,'NULLED!');
  --EXEC(@tmpsql);   -- comment out schema changing operation involving newly created table
END;

db<>fiddle demo - create insert trigger commented out

Trigger for insert is not created but there is no error.

vs.

db<>fiddle demo - create insert trigger forces 539 error

Schema changed after the target table was created. Rerun the Select Into query.

Outcome: It is rather not possible to inject "schema changing" operation in between SELECT * INTO ... FROM ...

Q: C/C++ standard string conversion functions don't support binary string literals? A:

AFAIK, strtol() and friends were introduced in C++11 and have not been substantively updated since. Binary integral literals were introduced in C++14.

Maybe that omission is an oversight. More likely, updating it hasn't been a high enough priority for someone and the committee to do the work (propose the change, assess there are no unintended consequences, champion the change through the vetting and review process, get it voted in). Those things are necessary before such changes can be introduced into a draft standard, let alone ratified.

That's what you get when a standard evolves over time, with a non-trivial process to get changes incorporated. There tends to be technical debt in the form of little omissions, oversights, and inconsistencies.

Q: What's the difference between RewriteRule and redirect 301 A:

RewriteRule is handled by Apache's mod_rewrite, while Redirect is handled by mod_alias. No, you don't need both.

Your RewriteRule (which uses regex) will not match /here (but will match such paths as /here/foo.html) because it is looking for a slash immediately after. You can make that optional by using a question mark:

RewriteRule ^here(/?.*) http://www.there.com$1 [R=301,L]

Now that will have the same effect as your Redirect. RewriteCond can be added to exclude certain paths:

RewriteCond $0 !/here/stayhere\.html

Note that some servers do not have mod_rewrite turned on by default. If adding RewriteEngine on to your configuration does not fix the problem and you cannot switch mod_rewrite on, at least mod_alias provides the RedirectMatch directive, which may be good enough:

RedirectMatch 301 ^/here(?!/stayhere\.html)(/?.*) http://www.there.com$1
